column3: Allah's knowledge of secret speech and private counsel directly supports the focus's source as Knower of the unseen.
It opposes truth to false covering while people know, but does not share the focus's projected truth image.
The divine attribute All-Knowing is shared, though the verse concerns bestowed favor rather than truth cast into conflict.
The messengers return unanswered histories to the One who alone fully knows the unseen.
The adjacent verse completes the same truth-falsehood contrast: when truth arrives, falsehood can neither initiate nor restore anything.
God recounts with knowledge and was never absent, closely reinforcing the focus's all-encompassing divine knowledge.
Truth is explicitly hurled against falsehood until it is crushed, the closest parallel to the focus's effective casting of truth.
The next verse likewise speaks in the prophetic command form and locates guidance in what the Lord reveals.
The Knower of the unseen controls disclosure of unseen knowledge, directly illuminating the focus's final divine attribute.
The prayer for judgment by truth shares the focus's truth as an effective divine act, without its casting image.
Truth's arrival and falsehood's disappearance directly parallel the focus's truth overcoming an ineffective rival.
It names a truth of certainty, supporting the firmness of haqq without the focus's conflict or transmission scene.
God's true command and knowledge of both unseen and seen closely join the two main claims of the focus.
It explicitly contrasts God as the true with what is called on besides Him as falsehood.
The repeated casting into water is a controlled, purposeful dispatch, but belongs to a distinct Moses narrative.
The same Lord and human lack of knowledge occur, but the subject is provision rather than truth and unseen knowledge.
Fear is cast into hearts with decisive effect, echoing the force of the focus's casting verb in a different setting.
A fulfilled promise makes God's truth known, but it does not develop the focus's unseen-knowing source.
The same surah joins judgment by truth to the All-Knowing Lord, though its scene is adjudication rather than casting.
It states a proposed legal recompense and has no material link to truth cast by the Knower of the unseen.
Knowing that revelation from the Lord is truth closely supports the focus's divinely sourced haqq.
The messenger stands on proof and God tells the truth, but the verse centers on judgment and delayed punishment.
Only God can originate and repeat creation, a close analogue to the focus's denial that falsehood can produce an effect.
Its unseen report is revealed history, not a positive connection to the focus's truth-projecting action.
Jesus distinguishes what he cannot know from the One who is Knower of all unseen things, directly matching the focus's attribute.
It contrasts God's guidance to truth with powerless rivals, strongly reinforcing the focus's true-versus-false polarity.
The exact formula Knower of the unseen and the seen directly supports the focus's divine knowledge claim.
The messenger does not know the timing of the promise, preparing the following affirmation that unseen knowledge belongs to God.
It concerns the excellence of creation and does not establish a relevant truth, casting, or unseen-knowledge relation.
It joins response to warning with reverence in the unseen, but concerns human faith rather than the divine Knower.
Return to the Knower of unseen and seen gives a direct eschatological use of the focus's divine attribute.
Divine aid and firmness for believers do not provide a specific relation to truth cast into falsehood.
The speakers limit their testimony to what they know and disclaim guardianship of the unseen, marking the human boundary implicit in the focus.
In the same surah, unbelievers cast assertions about the unseen from afar, a negative counterpart to the Lord casting truth.
God's beginning and repeating of creation faintly recalls the neighboring claim that falsehood cannot begin or repeat.
The statement that only the learned grasp parables does not create a sufficient relation to the focus.
The prophetic declaration of fearing the Lord shares the command form and Lord-reference but no central focus theme.
It explicitly calls idolatry fabricated falsehood and redirects provision and worship to God, supporting the focus's falsehood contrast.
The rhetorical question rejects a human claim to possess unseen knowledge, directly sharpening the focus's exclusive divine knowledge.
It repeats the prophet's fear of disobeying his Lord but has only a formal connection to the focus.
Disbelievers' disputation over signs is not specifically tied to truth's projection or hidden knowledge.
Return to the Knower of unseen and seen who discloses deeds closely matches the focus's all-knowing source.
Creation of heavens and earth in truth presents haqq as the ordered reality brought about by God.
It invokes the beginning of creation and its later renewal, but not the focus's truth-falsehood or unseen-knowledge themes.
The exact knowledge of unseen and seen grounds God's transcendence over alleged partners, closely fitting the focus.
Those who try to listen are cast away from every side, sharing the forceful casting image in a different scene.
The pursuing piercing flame continues the preceding expulsion scene, but the link to the focus is indirect.
The verse notes that most wrongdoers do not know, without developing unseen knowledge or truth's effective advance.
The people's repeated casting of ornaments exposes a chain of agency, but its object and meaning differ from casting truth.
What was sent down to Muhammad is explicitly truth from their Lord, supporting the source and content of the focus's haqq.
Conduct maintained in another's absence becomes knowable, echoing the distinction between hidden action and complete divine knowledge.
The Knower of unseen and seen is explicitly named as the great and exalted Judge, directly aligned with the focus.
The verse limits every human knower by a higher Knower, reinforcing the focus's unmatched divine knowledge.
God knows both what people conceal and announce, a direct expansion of the focus's knowledge of the unseen.
The exact formula Knower of unseen and seen provides a direct parallel to the focus's final clause.
It explicitly sets following falsehood against following truth from the Lord, closely matching the focus's polarity.
It describes ignorance of divinely revealed limits, but does not directly concern the unseen or truth's projection.
Noah's plea for help does not establish a material ayah-neighbour relation to the focus.
Opponents dispute with falsehood to dislodge truth, directly presenting the contested truth-falsehood field of the focus.
God's complete knowledge accompanies prior clarification of what people must avoid, linking knowledge to just divine guidance.
The command to pray to the Lord shares only the focus's prophetic address and divine reference.
Revelation is sent with God's knowledge and confirmed by divine witness, strongly supporting truth as sourced by complete knowledge.
Lot's plea against corrupt people has no specific connection to the focus's key themes.
Future knowledge follows heedless enjoyment, but the verse does not identify knowledge of the unseen or haqq.
Abraham's submission to his Lord shares the divine addressee but not the focus's thematic structure.
The Lord knows who has strayed and who is guided, supporting divine knowledge that exceeds limited human understanding.
The same surah and Lord-reference occur, but the subject is provision and replacement rather than truth or unseen knowledge.
The sleepers defer disputed knowledge of duration to their Lord, recognizing a human limit relevant to the focus's divine knowledge.
The Knower of unseen and seen is invoked as the one who judges disputes, directly combining the focus's attribute with effective truth.
Human knowledge can be gained and later lost within creation's stages, only broadly contrasting with the divine Knower.
God declares that He speaks truth, directly grounding the focus's haqq in the reliability of divine speech.
Each soul comes to know what it has brought, but this is personal disclosure rather than God's knowledge of the unseen.
It expressly restricts knowledge of the unseen in heavens and earth to God alone.
God knows the unseen of heavens and earth and sees deeds, strongly parallel to the focus's comprehensive knowledge.
The Holy Spirit brings revelation down from the Lord in truth, closely supporting the focus's divine truth transmission.
The promise of a knowing son resolves Abraham's fear, but has only a limited lexical connection to knowledge.
The same surah calls the Lord Knower of the unseen and says not even an atom escapes His knowledge.
The repeated warning that they will know is only a general future disclosure.
Teaching the Quran concerns divine communication, but does not specifically develop truth cast into a contested field.
Faith in the unseen concerns the human response to what is not seen, not the divine knowledge named in the focus.
The gathering of earlier and later people has no sufficiently specific relation to the focus.
The warning of future knowledge is a broad echo of disclosure, without the focus's unseen-knowing source.
Pharaoh's question about the Lord of the worlds does not supply a clear truth or unseen-knowledge connection.
Its repeated future knowledge warning remains a general disclosure motif rather than a close relation.
Teaching by the pen concerns imparted knowledge, but not the focus's divine knowledge of the unseen.
Nothing hidden in heaven or earth lies outside a clear record, closely reinforcing the focus's exhaustive divine knowledge.
God is the true King and the prophet asks for increased knowledge as revelation is completed, joining haqq and divine instruction.
God's hearing and knowledge ground refuge during provocation, but the setting is not truth cast against falsehood.
Judgment between all parties by truth parallels the focus's decisive divine haqq, without the unseen-knowledge formula.
The question denies that opponents possess the unseen or can authoritatively record it, directly echoing the focus's exclusive knowledge.
A concealed believer argues from clear signs and the Lord's claim, but this only loosely touches hiddenness and truth.
The townspeople assert control through a prior prohibition; the verse has no close truth or unseen-knowledge relation.
Their return to Hell has no specific thematic relation to the focus.
God's wisdom and knowledge across heaven and earth support His sole authority, though the unseen is not specified.
The generic punishment of criminals does not connect specifically to the focus's themes.
Teaching clear expression is a distant communication parallel, not a relation to truth projected by the Knower of unseen.
The morning cry that seizes the people lacks a specific link to the focus.
Seeing what was promised turns uncertainty into knowledge, complementing the surrounding discourse on human limits before the unseen.
God knows concealed self-betrayal before granting relief, a limited instance of divine knowledge of hidden conduct.
Competing groups contest whether Salih is sent by his Lord, but this does not closely develop the focus's truth or unseen knowledge.
It explicitly forbids mixing truth with falsehood and concealing truth while knowing, a direct omitted truth-falsehood parallel.
The keys of the unseen belong to God alone and nothing hidden escapes His knowledge, directly grounding the focus's final attribute.
Moses is commanded to cast his staff, which swallows the magicians' fabricated work, closely paralleling truth's decisive entry against falsehood.
Truth is made to prevail and the falsifiers' work is nullified, directly matching the focus's effective truth-falsehood contrast.
The messenger disclaims independent knowledge of the unseen, marking the creaturely boundary implied by the focus's exclusive divine knowledge.
God establishes truth and nullifies falsehood by His words, a direct formulation of the focus's victorious haqq.
God confirms truth by His words despite the criminals, closely paralleling truth as a divine force that overcomes opposition.
The unseen of the heavens and earth belongs to God, extending the focus's divine knowledge beyond the immediate conflict.
A report of the unseen is revealed to the prophet, showing hidden knowledge as dependent on divine disclosure.
The parable contrasts enduring truth with scum that vanishes, a major omitted articulation of truth's permanence over false appearance.
The unseen of heavens and earth belongs to God, directly reinforcing the focus's all-knowing divine source.
The truth is explicitly declared to be from the Lord, supporting the focus's divine origin of haqq.
Moses is told to cast what is in his hand so it swallows the artificers' work, a related scene of decisive overthrow of false production.
It declares that God is the Truth and gives life to the dead, grounding haqq in effective divine reality.
On the Day of judgment people will know that God is the manifest Truth, linking haqq to final disclosure.
Those given knowledge recognize what was sent down from the Lord as truth, a direct same-surah witness to revealed haqq.
God is Knower of the unseen of heavens and earth and knows what hearts contain, closely matching the focus's final predicate.
The Book is sent down from God in truth, directly supporting the focus's truth as divinely originating communication.
The Book is sent down to people in truth, another direct revelation-and-haqq parallel.
God judges by truth while alleged partners judge nothing, reinforcing the focus's contrast between effective divine haqq and impotence.
Falsehood cannot approach the revealed Book from before or behind, strongly complementing truth's power over falsehood.
God sends down the Book with truth and the balance, directly connecting divine revelation and haqq.
God erases falsehood and establishes truth by His words, one of the clearest omitted counterparts to the focus.
The messenger brings people the truth while most dislike it, preserving the focus's truth entering a resistant field.
Messengers, Book, and balance are sent so people may uphold justice, presenting revealed truth as an effective ordering force.
The messenger is sent with guidance and the religion of truth so it may prevail, extending the focus's victorious truth motif.
Whether speech is concealed or announced, God knows what is within hearts, directly reinforcing comprehensive knowledge of what is hidden.
The Creator's knowledge is affirmed as penetrating and fully aware, supporting the focus's claim that the source of truth knows what is unseen.
